column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words in all; beyond the description it adds only a short legislative history of the 1903 bill

The article contradicts itself on which tens belong to which line: the lead says the second to sixth tens concern the Imayavaramban rulers, the Contents section says the second to fifth, with the sixth to eighth on the Irumporai. The text says only second to fifth (Imayavaramban) and seventh and eighth (Irumporai). The article names Perunceral Irumporai as the subject of both the eighth and the ninth ten, though only eight tens survive (first and last lost); left out. The article says the fourth ten's poet received four million gold coins; left out as an unsupported-looking figure. The entry spells the king Senguttuvan; the article Cenkuttuvan (used here, no contradiction).

The article dates the grant of Albarracín between 1166 and 1168, or perhaps as late as 1169-70; the entry says around 1170. No date given in the text. The patron's name is left out (article Muhammad ibn Mardanis, entry Ibn Mardanish); the entry already names him.

The entry says trials ran from December 1944; the article gives only the start of the verdicts on 1 February 1945. Both kept, no contradiction. Mushanov's death on 21 May 1951 'in the cabinet of a doctor at Darzhavna sigurnost' left out as unclear.

Spelling: the entry has Yevhenia Bosh, the article Yevgenia Bosch / Bosch. The entry's spelling is used; the checker may flag it. The article's last section is cut off mid-list of the Povstanburo members.

The article dates the war 1875-1877 in its lead (the hanging of Lela Pandak Lam was in 1877), but says the war ended by mid-1876; the entry has 1875-1876. No end year and no year for the hanging are given in the text. The article is confused on Captain Innes (killed at Bandar Tua on 7 November, and again in the first attack on Pasir Salak on 15 November) and dates the capture of Pasir Salak to 12 December after an arrival on 15 November; these details are left out. The entry calls the killer the Maharaja Lela; the article Lela Pandak Lam (used here).
The article contradicts itself on the date of the 1853 treaty: its lead says it was signed in August 1853 at Basidu and Bushire, its body gives 4 May 1853. No day or month is given in the text.

The entry says he outlived his son; the article says both his sons, Philipp the Younger and Eberhard, died before him. The text names both, which does not deny the entry's statement. The article calls Henry III 'margrave' once and 'Landgrave' elsewhere; the entry's Landgrave is used.

The article does not give the year of his commission of 20 February (after sailing on 12 January 1638); left without a date. The entry says governor from 1639, which the article's lead also gives. The article has two contradictory accounts of St Croix (bought by Poincy and bequeathed to the knights, and captured from the Spanish in 1650); left out. The entry spells the island Saint Christophe; the article St Kitts / Saint Christopher. St Kitts used.
The article dates the stupa c. 1560 and the kings' decision c. 1556; the entry gives 1560-1563. The text gives only the decision around 1556 and no completion date.
The article gives his life as c. 1750 - c. 1799; the entry has only 18th century (consistent).
The article contradicts itself: its lead says the plan was proclaimed by Obregón, its body that Obregón signed on only after the plan was issued. The text does not say who proclaimed it.

The article says Díaz assumed the presidency on 12 May 1877 as the only candidate, and that Iglesias was appointed interim president after Tecoac; the entry says Díaz took Mexico City after Tecoac and became president. The date and the interim arrangement are left out. The article says Díaz entered Puebla in November 1876, the entry Mexico City; left out.
SKIPPED: article is a short lead and a list of dukes, too thin for a longer text; its lead also gives the duchy's spans inconsistently (second state to 1523 in the lead, absorbed in 1478 in the text)
The entry dates the Treaty of Asurar Ali to 1639; the article gives no year. No year in the text.
The article gives his birth as 5 June 1929 in the lead and 25 June 1929 in the text; only the year is given here.

The heroine is called Sanyogita and Samyogita in the article's plot summary, Samyukta once elsewhere; the entry has Samyukta. The text avoids naming her. The article says some scholars date the oldest version to the 13th century; the entry says surviving versions date from the 16th century or later (consistent: only the scholars' view of the core is given).

The entry credits Prola with defeating and capturing the Chalukya king Taila III. The article says the Tailapa he captured was Kumara Tailapa, brother of Someshvara III and governor of Kanduru-nadu, and that the older identification with Tailapa III has little evidence. The episode is left out of the text. The article dates his death around 1157 or 1158; the entry's reign ends c. 1157. No year of death given in the text.

The entry calls the union inaugurated on 30 March 1949 the United State of Greater Rajasthan; the article calls the 30 March 1949 union Greater Rajasthan and gives the name United States of Greater Rajasthan to the union formed on 15 May 1949 with the Matsya Union. The text names neither for those two steps. The article says the day fell on 19 March in 2026; left out, as the entry gives 30 March and the article gives no reason.

Dates left out: the entry gives his father's death around 605 and his own death around 606. The article says R. C. Majumdar dates the father's death and Rajyavardhana's accession to 604, Kaushik Roy to 606 and some sources to 605; it gives his reign as 605 to 606 and his death as later in 606. The entry states that Shashanka killed him; the article says he was perhaps murdered by Shashanka. The text gives whose account that is without adding a figure.
The article says only that he retired on pension; the entry's 1903 end of office agrees with the retirement date of 1 October 1903.

The article's paragraph on the queen, Lakhan Thapa Magar and the Manakamana Temple is confused and was left out. The article gives the Mahabharat Range as the western limit as well as the Marshyangdi; only the Trishuli and Marshyangdi limits are used.
Dates left out: the entry gives his death as c. 1423 (in the 1420s); the article gives 1428 and a reign as 12th Rao of Marwar from 1384 to 1428.
SKIPPED: the article is a list of office holders with a three-sentence lead; it adds nothing to the description
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (ethnic groups, a disputed massacre toll, a fruit monument and a list of sights)

The entry says tenants traded furs under the patroon's authority; the article says fur trading was illegal for colonists, a West India Company monopoly. Fur trade left out of the text. The article calls Stephen III both the last patroon and Stephen IV the tenth and last patroon; the text names no last patroon.
SKIPPED: different subject: the entry is the Riau Malay language, the article is about the Riau Malay people, with only a short section on the language

The article's genealogy and its praise of Moody's character are left out. It calls him the first lieutenant governor of British Columbia, a title the entry does not use; left out. Retirement places as the article names them.

The entry gives his reign as 1911 to 1923 and an abdication in 1923 after a dispute with Patiala; the article says he was forced to give up control to a British administrator in 1923 on suspicion of kidnapping and attempted poisoning, and that he was formally deposed in 1928, giving his reign as 1911 to 1928. The text gives neither the reason for 1923 nor a reign end date; it says only what happened in 1923 and 1928. The article places his council service of 1906-08 once in the Imperial Legislative Council and once in the Punjab Legislative Council; the text says only the legislative council. The Jaito protest named in the entry is not in the article.
The text writes Roca Jr. and Sir Walter Runciman as the article does; the entry's lede calls Runciman the British trade minister.
SKIPPED: different subject: the article is about Roque Lopez Duarte, a Spanish sculptor (1747-1811), a namesake of the Filipino revolutionary

The article gives the earldom both as letters patent of 4 September 1603 and as created on 29 September 1603; the text gives no day. The article gives Hugh Roe's death in Spain as 30 August (old style) or 9 September (new style) 1602; the text says only 1602.

The entry spells the name Rory Óg O'More; the article writes Rory Oge O'More. The text follows the entry. The article says he was 'considered the greatest obstacle' to Elizabeth I's conquest of the midlands without attribution; left out.
The entry says he was patronised by a minister of the king; the article places him at the court of Veera Ballala II and adds the minister as a patron. Both are kept as the article gives them.

The article says the day commemorates the Sardinian Vespers of 1794 to 1796; the entry ties it to the rising of 28 April 1794. The text follows both, without saying one or the other is the official meaning. The article's claim that Sardinia was the first European country to make a revolution of its own is unattributed and was left out.

The entry spells the name Sabagadis Woldu; the article's title is Subagadis Woldu, though it uses Sabagadis in the text. The article says he ruled Tigray and the Eritrean coastal plains by 1818 but also that he won the Tigrayan overlordship in 1822; the text follows 1822, as the entry does. The article gives his birth year as 1780; left out, as the entry gives only his death. The article mentions Dejazmatch Hagos Subagadis being beaten to death on 15 February; the text gives no day for the executions.

The entry says Gorton founded Shawomet in 1642; the article says he and 11 others bought the land from Miantonomi in January 1643. The year of the purchase is left out of the text. The entry says he secured protection from Parliament; the article names the Commissioner of Plantations and a letter of protection from the Earl of Warwick. The text names only the Earl's letter, which does not contradict the entry.

The entry says he lived among the Oneida from 1766; the article places his move to central New York after he parted from Wheelock in 1770. The year he began living among the Oneida is left out of the text. His death on 28 February 1808 is given only in the article's lead, so the last heading is Legacy.

The article says nothing of conspiracies suppressed in Santo Domingo, mentioned in the entry; nothing in the text contradicts it. The article calls him a colonel in its lead and brigadier and field marshal later; the text gives only the later ranks with their dates.
The article calls Université Laval the first Catholic French-language university in North America; the entry says the first French-language university. The text does not repeat either claim.

The article's lead says the tribe has owned the Hard Rock Cafe since 2006; its economic section says it bought the franchise in 2007, as the entry does. The text does not repeat the purchase. Left out: the present chairman, wealth estimates 'as of 2016', and the 2021 sports-betting litigation.
The article is short (about 300 words of substance); the text keeps to what it gives beyond the entry and runs to two sections.
Left out the article's ranking of the college as the fourth oldest in India and its current accreditation grade.
The article's lead and the opening of each section only; the essays on the economic bases of the Republic and the Catholic conquest have no text in the file.

The article dates the work to 1260 CE without a hedge; the entry says around 1260. The text gives no year. The article renders the title 'The Jewel Mirror of Language', the entry 'jewel-mirror of grammar'; the text does not translate the title. Diacritics of names (Kēśirāja, Liṅgaṇārādhya, Niṣṭhūra) are given plainly as the entry writes Kesiraja; the checker may flag some of these spellings.

The article gives no date for the stone; the entry's 'around 800 CE' is neither repeated nor contradicted. The article spells the Gaelic name both Clach a' Charridh and Clach a' Charaidh; the text does not repeat it.

The entry says most of the fort was pulled down in 1969; the article says the demolition took place in January 1970. The text gives no year for the demolition. The article is short (about 350 words); the text runs to two sections.
The entry gives 258 for Liwei's settlement as tradition; the article says only the mid-3rd century. The text keeps the article's wording, which does not contradict the entry.
The article's Aftermath spells the viceroy both Elliot and Elliott; the text uses Sir Gilbert Elliot.
The article is short (about 450 words); the text runs to two sections.

The article (titled Simhana) disputes the start of the reign: inscriptions suggest 1200, 1207, 1208-09 or 1210; A. S. Altekar holds he succeeded in 1210 after being heir apparent from 1200, T. V. Mahalingam that he was crowned in 1200 and again in 1210. The entry says c. 1210; the text gives no year of accession. The end of the reign is also disputed: Altekar November or December 1246, Mahalingam the last quarter of 1247. The entry says c. 1246; the text gives no year. Spellings follow the entry: Singhana (article mostly Simhana) and Sharngadeva (article Sharanga-deva); the checker may flag them. Left out: the article's mention of the Muslim conquest half a century after his death, which needs a dated source.
The article names a writer, Hawn, on cyclical forms without saying who he is; the text gives the point without the name.

SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry (torcs, Great Torc, Iceni, British Museum); the rest (wear analysis, a votive hypothesis, a separate Roman jeweller's hoard) would not fill 260 words without padding

SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, much of it already in the entry, and it is inconsistent about where the Yashastilaka was written (in the domain of Vagaraj, a feudatory of Krishna III, and also at Gangadhara under the Vemulavada Chalukya Baddega II); not enough sound material for 260 words

The article reports two versions of the end of the reign: the Sinnamanur plates say Srimara repelled Sena II and Maya Pandya; other records that he died of wounds after his capital was taken; Nilakanta Sastri and later epigraphists favour a successful defence. The entry says he was defeated by a Sri Lankan counter-invasion. The text says only that accounts differ, naming no outcome. The article contradicts itself on the dissident prince: it identifies Maya Pandya with Varaguna II, yet also names Varaguna II as Srimara's elder son who succeeded him at once. The text leaves the identification out. Left out: the claimed encounter with the Pala Empire (most historians treat it as courtly hyperbole).

The end of the reign is uncertain in the article: the lead gives 844/45 to c. 870/71, with Rama Rajasekhara succeeding c. 870/71, yet the view it calls generally supported (Elamkulam P. N. Kunjan Pillai's) has Sthanu Ravi ruling until about 885 to join Aditya Chola's Kongu conquest. The entry says c. 844-883. The text gives no end date. M. G. S. Narayanan, following T. V. Mahalingam, identifies Rajakesari Varma with Srikantha Chola (817-845) and dates the Kongu action to 844/45; the entry names Aditya I, so the text gives only the view recent scholarship supports. The article dates the Quilon plates around 849, in line with the entry's 849; the text gives the regnal year only.

The article also says a Kachari princess was suspected along with Suklenmung; left out as the sentence is garbled. General Ton-kham's pursuit to the Karatoya is in the lead; the body gives the pursuit without his name, so only the Bharali battle is told.

Article: deposed by the Saudi Amir as head of the Qawasim soon after May 1808 and as ruler of Ras Al Khaimah 'the following year' (1809); worded without the exact year. Born 1781 per article; entry gives only d. 1866, so the birth year is left out but the age at death (85) kept. Article spells the Saudi appointee both Hassan bin Rahma and Hassan bin Rahmah.
Article is a list page with about 450 words of prose; written in two sections. Entry spells Muhammad Bello; article Muhammed Bello (the entry's spelling used).

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 300 words of loosely connected myth notes, partly garbled; it does not support the entry's Tu'i Manu'a and lineage points and adds little that would make 260 words without padding

Entry spells Mayurasharma and Shantivarma; the article has Mayurasarman and Santivarman (entry spellings used). The article's verse 11 has a quarrel with a Pallava horseman; the entry says guard, so the quarrel itself is not retold.
SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words, most of it already in the entry (born in Shuri, five journeys to Edo and Kagoshima, udui bugyo from 1715, the names of the five plays are all it adds)

SKIPPED: article too thin (about 230 words). Also for the editor: the article has him succeed his brother Naulivou Ramatenikutu as 5th Vunivalu in 1832 and be overthrown the same year, restored in 1837; the entry says he was Vunivalu from the late 1820s.
Entry calls him a muleteer and blacksmith; article agrees. The 1858-1859 dating in the entry is matched by the December 1858 choice as leader and the January 1859 rising.
Line count left out: the entry says some 13,000 lines, the article just under 14,000. The article dates Ramsay's transcription to 1489 only in a text heading; left out.

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 330 words, and beyond the entry it adds only a quotation from the introduction, Conan Doyle's view of the Belgian annexation, one Daily Express review and a 2009 reprint

The entry says he sided with the Crown 'including at Kinsale in 1601'; the article says he sailed south with 300 men in three ships and kept both sides guessing whom he would help. Kinsale left out of the text. The article names his wife's father both Donal O'Conor Sligo and Charles O'Conor Sligo; father's name left out.
The article gives no year for his arrival in the Khasi Hills (the entry says 1841); not stated in the text.

The article's lead places the viscountcy after his exile; its body dates it to 1650, before he left Ireland in 1652. Worded so as not to place it. Family section is confused (a daughter born 1624 by a second wife); only the wife and heir kept.

The article's figures for the Thomas contingent disagree with each other (600 teachers; 346 men and 180 women; nearly 500; 365 men and 165 women); the entry says over five hundred. No figure given in the text. Act No. 74 dated both 20 and 21 January 1901 in the article; 21 January used, as in its fuller sentence. The 'third largest English-speaking nation' claim left out as a ranking.
The entry calls the third kingdom Di; the article Zhai (entry spelling used, may be flagged).
The entry's point that Abbas I paid them from the royal treasury is not in the article; not repeated or contradicted.
Weight left out: the entry says over 20 kg, the article just over 23 kg (consistent, but not repeated). The entry's more than 250 pieces and the Votadini are not in the article.
The article calls Ferdinand their brother; the entry half-brother. Neither word used in the text beyond naming the mothers.

The entry places Daan north-west of Sanaa; the article says north of Amran (both can be true). The text says only north of Amran. The article names the imam Yahya Muhammad Hamid ed-Din; the text uses Imam Yahya. The article gives the signing as 18 October 1911 (body) and October 1911 (lead); both agree with the entry's 1911.
The entry's hostages are not in the article; the text does not mention them.

Date: the entry gives 30 September 1809; the article says the treaty was signed on 29 September 1809. The signing day is left out. Area: the entry says about three million acres; the article's body says over 3,000,000 acres but its lead says 29,719,530 acres. No figure is given in the text. The article also calls it the Ten O'clock Line Treaty and the Twelve Mile Line Treaty; left out for length.
The article gives the ceded area as 6,283,804 acres; not used, for length.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry's description
The entry says Mountjoy had the chair destroyed in 1602; the article says he smashed the inauguration stone, then part of the chair. The destruction is not retold.
The article credits him with being one of the first 20th-century leaders to use nonviolent resistance against colonial rule; left out as an assessment.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it also has the Germans proclaiming him king in April 1885 and his rule running 1886-1889, against the entry's installation in 1887

The entry dates Ah Kukum Xiu's submission to 1542; the article dates only the first Xiu envoys to Montejo, around 1539, and names no submission year. The text gives the envoys only. The article spells the rival group both Capul and Copul; both kept as the article has them in each sentence.

The entry spells the founding chief John Deseronto; the article has John Deserontyon. The entry's spelling is used, so the checker may flag it. The entry says the settlers came from the Mohawk valley; the article names Fort Hunter, New York. The text names Fort Hunter only. Left out as present-day and passing: the boil-water advisory of 2008, radio stations.
The article says he divorced his first wife although hers was the only marriage declared valid; the divorce is left out.
The entry dates his rule to around 1500; the article says only the sixteenth century. No date is given in the text. His death is not told in the article, so the last section is headed Legacy.

The excerpt does not cover the refused visit to New Zealand of 1985 that the entry describes, so the text does not retell it. The medal's name is given as the article has it (Armed Services Expeditionary Forces Medal).
Climate figures and present employers left out as padding.

The entry bounds the vale by the Pennines and the North York Moors; the article names the Howardian Hills and Yorkshire Wolds to the east. The eastern boundary is left out of the text. The entry's Anglian and Viking settlement is not in the article; not retold.

Dates: the entry places the defeat at Sripurambiyam around 885; the article dates his reign c. 862 to c. 879, the defeat around 879 and the battle c. 880, and his brother's succession around 880. No year is given in the text. The article spells the battle Sri Purambiyam and Shripurambiyam; the entry's Sripurambiyam is used, which the checker may flag. The article spells the Pallava king Nrupatunga varman and Nripatunga and the Ganga king Prithivipati I and Prithvipati I; the text keeps the article's forms. The article once identifies Maya Pandya with Varaguna II in brackets; left out as unclear. His death is not told in the article; the text ends with his succession.

The entry says he was killed in a clash with Soviet forces; the article says he shot himself during a fight with a squadron of Red Cossacks. The text says only that he died in the fight. The entry says the republic controlled some twenty villages; the article says 25. No figure is given. The entry's Motronynskyi Monastery is not in the article.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance

The article dates his reign c. 971-998; consistent with the entry's 10th century, but not given in the text. The entry says he broke free of the Gurjara-Pratiharas; the article says his father Simharaja had already taken an imperial title and that Vigraharaja was probably the first truly independent king. The text gives the father's title only. His death is not told, so the last section is headed Legacy.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, and its reign dates (3 BCE to 32 CE in the lead, 12 BCE to about 20 CE in the body) disagree with each other and with the entry's 1st century BCE
The article gives a reign of about 62 years; not printed as a figure, since the entry dates the reign c. 1097–1160. The article spells Vijaya Sena; the entry's Vijayasena is used.
Death left out: the article dates him c. 1590–c. 1670s; Makrand Mehta thinks he died in 1670, B. G. Gokhale and Paul Dundas 1675; the entry has c. 1670 and 'last recorded in 1670'.
The article has no history section (no Kīngitanga history, raupatu or 1995 settlement), so the text covers the tribe's make-up and government only.
Left out the article's ambiguous clause on which side 'bore the main burden of the war' after Brissac's invasion of Piedmont.

The article dates the founding of the State of Muskogee to 1795 and seems to put his capture and Madrid captivity after the war of 1800; the entry has him escape Spanish captivity and proclaim the state on his return in 1799. The founding year is left out and the Madrid episode told before the state, as in the entry. The article gives his age as thirteen on joining the battalion and 16 or 17 in 1781 (inconsistent); ages left out. Some sources give his birth as 1764.
The article says Courteen sent a few colonists to Barbados in 1625; the entry dates the first settlement to 1627. The 1625 date is left out.

The article gives his first governorships as 1643 (lead) and as 1641–1642 and 1643–1644 (body); written as 'the early 1640s'. The article dates the Eleuthera voyage only to between 1646 and 1648 and calls the dates uncertain; the entry has 1648, so no voyage year is printed.
The article has him Ras of Tigray from 1788 (and regent 1797–1800); the entry has 'from about 1790'. Only the 1790 grant of titles, which both support, is printed.

The article dates the famine 1972–1975, says it ravaged the provinces by early 1972 and killed 40,000–80,000 in 1972 and 1973, and cites an estimate of 250,000 dead by 1975; the entry dates it 1973–1974. The famine's start and end years and the 250,000 figure are left out.

The section 'His place in Andalusia' is a garbled machine translation (Malik calling him 'the sane of Andalusia', the Rabad revolt) and was not used beyond the plain statement that he was accused of taking part in a rising.
Short article (about 300 words of substance); text kept near the lower limit.

Disagreements with the entry left out: the article dates his death to November 1638 (lead: c. 1640), the entry to 1637; and the article has Yusuf defending Mombasa against the 1632 expedition, which lifted its siege on 15 March, before leaving the town, while the entry says he abandoned the town before the relief force arrived. The siege's course and the death year are not printed. The article also has him 11 years old in 1614 though born c. 1607, and ruler 'from 1614 to 1632'; both left out. The article spells the people Mussungoro, Musongoro and Musungoro; Musungoro used.

The article has Yidougui flee to the northern desert and later move to Goguryeo, where he remained for the rest of his life; the entry has him die in the steppe in 344. Goguryeo is left out. The Book of Wei dates his defeat to 345; the entry's 344 is used.

The article says the group's name came from their battle axes (Nzappa zap), while the entry says they were named after their leader; the origin of the name is left out. The entry says they sacked the Kuba capital Nsheng in 1899; the article places the 1899 massacre in the Pyang region and says the colonial authorities only established a post in the royal capital in 1910; neither the sack nor 1910 is printed.
The article spells the name Abhiyaza (Abhirājā); the entry's spelling Abhiraja is used throughout and may be flagged.

The article dates his death to 1876, the entry to 1877; no death year is printed. The article's account of an uprising against the British 'in 1862' under his leadership (placed among events of the 1830s) is muddled and left out, as is its statement that he took direct control of the state of Swat in the 1850s, which sits uneasily with the entry's statement that his grandson founded the state.

The article says the fort was built by the Ruler of Sharjah (the agreement has him build the rest house with funds advanced by the company) and that the fortified rest house was not finished until 1937, the first passengers sleeping in tents; the entry says Imperial Airways built it in 1932. The builder and the completion date are left out. The article says it was restored in the late 1990s, the entry 'restored in 2000'; only the opening of 14 March 2000 is printed. 'As of June 2025 closed for renovation' left out.
The entry calls him a scholar of Zaydi law; the article does not cover this, so it is not mentioned. Hadramawt spelt as the entry has it; the article writes Hadramaut.

The entry's legal disputes with the Thakores of Palitana are not in the article and are not told. Left out the present head (Samveg Lalbhai) and the annual repair spending of Rs 150 million as present-day figures.
The entry's claim that he began the mole and new defences of Tangier is not in the article and is not repeated.
The entry dates the rediscovery to 1987; the article gives 1988. The year is left out of the text.

The entry speaks of an early kingdom of Dunoding formed with Eifionydd; the article calls Dunoding a sub-kingdom (cantref) of which Ardudwy was a division. The text calls it the cantref of Dunoding, as the article does. Left out 'as of 2024'.

The article dates the burials from the latter part of the 1st millennium BCE to the Roman conquest, about 70 CE; consistent with the entry's dates. Many finds are in the Yorkshire Museum and the British Museum (not used).

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance, most of it about his father Raden Kikin, Pati Unus and Trenggana; a text of 260 words would be padded. The article spells his name Panangsang in its body and calls him king of Demak 1549-1554; the entry says he claimed the throne in the succession war.
The article does not tell his death, only his deposition in 1599, so no death section is written.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance (the name's etymology, his family from two inscriptions, one coin type); a full text would be padded. The article argues that he probably ruled in the middle of the 1st century CE and says his father Indravarma ruled in 50 CE; the entry dates him to the early 1st century CE. The entry places the dynasty at Bajaur; the article says he ruled in Gandhara.

The entry says the experiment lasted until Aundh's merger into India in 1948; the article says it ended with independence in 1947. No year is given for the end. The article dates Patwardhan's hiding during Quit India to 1946 (the movement began in 1942); the year is left out. The entry's spelling Bhawanrao is used; the article has Bhavanrao Srinivasrao. The article says Gandhi and Frydman drafted the November Declaration; the month is not used.

The article gives the repeal's commencement date as '3 April 150', a slip; no date is given in the text. Leatham is said in the article to have introduced the act 'on leave'; worded as introducing the bill.

The entry stresses imported Mediterranean amphorae of the 5th and 6th centuries and the tin trade with the Byzantine world; the article speaks of tin sold to the Gauls in Roman times and a settlement lasting into post-Roman times. The text keeps to the article without dating the post-Roman phase.

The article's statement that the legal basis for slavery was established in Mexico in 1636 looks like a slip and is not used. The article's summary puts whipping, slitting of the nose and burning on a first offence and death on the next; the code's text it quotes puts the mutilation on the second offence.
